comparison: Perfect agreement on water drinking baseline data (C18, C23, C24, C31, C33). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found these claims supported with no concerns raised about the statistical analyses or conclusions.

Disagreement on alcohol consumption equivalence claims (C25, C26, C27). OpenEval found claims supported by appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers expressed uncertainty about whether equivalent volume consumption reflects equivalent intoxication, questioning if body size differences confound interpretation.

Disagreement on drinking efficiency claims (C19, C32, C34, C36). OpenEval found the 'efficiency' interpretation supported by statistical evidence of sex differences in bout duration and drinks per bout. Peer reviewers questioned whether this reflects true efficiency or simply body size differences, and noted inconsistencies across analytic domains.

Agreement on temporal drinking measures (C35, C37). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accepted these findings showing no sex differences in specific temporal aspects of drinking behavior, with appropriate statistical support.

Disagreement on water drinking temporal changes in males (C52, C53, C54). OpenEval found claims supported by appropriate statistical analyses showing week effects. Peer Reviewer 3 specifically questioned the interpretation and meaning of these temporal changes during baseline water phase.

Disagreement on female circuit stability claims (C57, C62). OpenEval found claims supported by data showing no changes across weeks in females. Peer reviewers expressed uncertainty, questioning whether individual variation in female drinking behavior maps to circuit activity and noting inconsistencies in reconciling photometry with behavioral data.

Agreement on lateralization novelty (C58, C59, C60). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly supported the lateralization findings as novel and important. Editor and reviewers provided 'solid evidence' assessment and emphasized fundamental importance for the field.

Both express concerns about sex-specific predictive relationship claims (C28, C29, C30). OpenEval rated as UNCERTAIN due to potential p-hacking concerns with a priori sex separation despite non-significant ANCOVA. Peer reviewers did not directly address but editor noted 'other evidence is incomplete' and inconsistencies in reconciling data.

Partial overlap on male circuit engagement claims (C22, C55, C56, C61). OpenEval found claims supported by statistical evidence and integration with prior optogenetic work. Peer reviewers expressed uncertainty about interpretation of temporal changes and noted lack of causal evidence, with Reviewer 3 specifically questioning what the water-drinking changes mean.

Strong agreement on lateralization findings (C38, C39, C40, C41, C49, C50, C51). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found extensive support for lateralized, sex-specific effects. Editor stated 'solid evidence' and reviewers praised the novel discovery and exhaustive analysis of bilateral recordings.

Agreement on right hemisphere lateralization effects (C44, C45, C46, C47, C48). Both evaluations supported these findings as part of the broader lateralization discovery. OpenEval found appropriate statistical support; peer reviewers acknowledged comprehensive bilateral analysis without specific concerns.

Agreement on temporal shift findings (C42, C43). OpenEval found strong statistical support for sex-specific temporal shifts in calcium dynamics. Peer reviewers supported these as part of the lateralization evidence, with no specific challenges raised.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretation (C61). OpenEval found the integration of decreased calcium activity with prior optogenetic work to be appropriately supported. Peer reviewers expressed uncertainty, with Reviewer 1 noting 'no causal link between activity in the pathway and drinking has been established here' and editor stating 'findings would benefit from causal assessment.'

OpenEval evaluated background/public health claims (C1, C2, C3, C4) as supported by appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not comment on standard background citations.

OpenEval evaluated experimental model validity claims (C5, C6, C7, C8) as supported by appropriate literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not challenge the choice or validity of the DID model.

OpenEval evaluated claims about sex differences complexity in literature (C9, C10, C11, C12) as supported by multiple citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not dispute the characterization of prior literature on sex differences.

OpenEval evaluated knowledge gap and rationale claims (C13, C14) as supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not challenge the study rationale or literature gap identification.

OpenEval evaluated claims about authors' prior work (C15, C16, C17) as appropriately supported by self-citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not question the foundation from previous studies.

OpenEval evaluated methodological claims (C63-C70) as supported with appropriate technical details and transparency. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not raise concerns about the fiber photometry methods or quality control procedures.
